title: Gastrointestinal System and Liver
tagline: Digestion and absorption, the oesophagus, stomach and bowel, the liver, the pancreas and biliary tract, and clinical nutrition
summary: The gut digests and absorbs food, and the liver processes what is absorbed. This course covers the physiology of digestion, disorders of the oesophagus, stomach and bowel, gastrointestinal bleeding and cancer, liver tests and liver disease, the pancreas and biliary tract, and clinical nutrition.
overview: The gastrointestinal tract moves, secretes, digests and absorbs: it takes in food and about 2 litres of drink a day, adds about 7 litres of its own secretions, and returns almost all of it to the body. The liver then processes what has been absorbed, makes most plasma proteins and clears drugs and bilirubin. Diseases of the system present with a fairly short list of symptoms, such as pain, a change in bowel habit, bleeding, vomiting, jaundice, weight loss and difficulty swallowing, and the pattern of these symptoms often points to the organ involved.

The course starts with the physiology of motility, secretion, digestion and absorption, including the enterohepatic circulation and the mechanisms of diarrhoea. It then works through the oesophagus and stomach (dysphagia, reflux, Helicobacter pylori and peptic ulcer), the small and large bowel (coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease and appendicitis), and gastrointestinal bleeding and cancer, including bowel cancer screening. Two chapters cover the liver: how to read liver tests and approach jaundice, and the causes and complications of liver disease. The pancreas and biliary tract follow, and a final chapter covers malnutrition, refeeding syndrome, enteral and parenteral nutrition and obesity.

Each chapter combines mechanisms with worked clinical cases and simple calculations, such as the faecal osmotic gap, the Glasgow–Blatchford score, the R ratio, FIB-4, MELD, the serum–ascites albumin gradient and nutritional requirements. Management is described in principle and refers to current UK guidance from NICE and the British Society of Gastroenterology, with international guidance where it is standard.
outcomes: Explain the motility, secretion, digestion and absorption of each region of the gut, their neural and hormonal control, and the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts.
Classify diarrhoea as osmotic, secretory, inflammatory or motility-related, and use the faecal osmotic gap and the pattern of deficiencies to localise malabsorption.
Evaluate dysphagia, reflux and dyspepsia, explain the role of Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs in peptic ulcer, and recognise the alarm features that require urgent endoscopy.

Compare Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, recognise acute severe colitis, and describe the diagnosis and management of coeliac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, diverticulitis and appendicitis.
Assess and outline the management of upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding, including risk scoring, and describe the investigation of iron deficiency and the principles of bowel cancer screening.
Interpret liver blood tests as patterns of injury, cholestasis and synthetic failure, and work through the causes of jaundice.
Describe the main causes of liver disease and the complications of cirrhosis, including portal hypertension, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, encephalopathy and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Diagnose gallstone disease, cholangitis and acute pancreatitis, grade the severity of pancreatitis, and recognise the presentation of pancreatic and biliary cancer.
Screen for malnutrition, estimate energy, protein and fluid requirements, prevent refeeding syndrome, and choose between oral, enteral and parenteral nutrition.

history.title: A window into the stomach
history.detail: A gunshot wound leaves Alexis St Martin with a permanent opening into his stomach. The army surgeon William Beaumont uses it over the next decade to sample gastric juice and observe digestion directly, publishing his experiments in 1833.

history.title: Looking inside the stomach
history.detail: Adolf Kussmaul passes a rigid tube into the stomach of a professional sword-swallower, an early demonstration that the upper gut could be inspected directly.

history.title: Secretin, the first hormone
history.detail: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling show that acid in the duodenum triggers pancreatic secretion through a substance carried in the blood, which they call secretin. Starling later introduces the word "hormone".

history.title: The nervous control of digestion
history.detail: Ivan Pavlov receives the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the nervous control of digestive secretion, including the cephalic phase of gastric secretion.

history.title: The flexible endoscope
history.detail: Basil Hirschowitz and colleagues test the first fibreoptic gastroscope, which makes inspection and biopsy of the upper gut routine.

history.title: The Australia antigen
history.detail: Baruch Blumberg identifies an antigen later shown to be the surface protein of hepatitis B virus, leading to diagnostic tests and vaccines. He shares the 1976 Nobel Prize.

history.title: Liver transplantation
history.detail: After a first attempt in 1963, Thomas Starzl in Denver performs the first liver transplant with prolonged survival. Roy Calne in Cambridge later develops the European programme.

history.title: Helicobacter pylori
history.detail: Robin Warren and Barry Marshall in Perth culture a spiral bacterium from gastric biopsies and propose that it causes gastritis and peptic ulcer. Eradication therapy turns ulcer disease into a curable infection, and they receive the Nobel Prize in 2005.

history.title: Hepatitis C is identified
history.detail: Michael Houghton and colleagues clone the genome of the main cause of non-A, non-B hepatitis. Harvey Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles Rice share the 2020 Nobel Prize, and direct-acting antivirals now cure most infections.
